Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Civil Servant
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Vignette:
Three years ago, during a routine compliance inspection at a federal environmental facility, Clara Vance stood in a sublevel corridor when the ventilation system failed. Without warning, the air grew thick and acrid, carrying a sharp, chemical tang that stung her throat and eyes. Alarms blared. People rushed past, shouting orders in overlapping, rapid-fire dialects that bled into one another. She remembered the floor vibrating under her boots, the way the vapor curled around the doorframes, and the sudden, suffocating pressure in her chest. She was pulled to safety, but the moment left no clear narrative in her mind—only a dense, wordless picture of panic and a body that had reacted before her thoughts could catch up. In the months that followed, Clara’s world narrowed. She had come to believe that stability could only exist behind her kitchen door or within the small reading nook in her bedroom. Anything beyond those two rooms felt unmoored, liable to collapse into chaos at a moment’s notice. At work, where she spent her days as a civil servant managing case files in a bustling municipal office, the environment grew increasingly hostile. The open-plan layout meant corridors constantly filled with colleagues speaking in rapid, clipped phrases. Their overlapping chatter never resolved into clear words, just a relentless blur of syllables that left her grasping for meaning. When new supervisors arrived or emergency drills interrupted her schedule, she would freeze, her hands gripping her desk until her knuckles turned white. Unpredictability stopped being a mere inconvenience; it became a signal that danger was already present. She began to rehearse every sentence before speaking, tracing the same polite, professional responses in her head until her jaw ached. If someone approached her desk with an unexpected query, she would deflect, citing paperwork, until they moved on. Strangers—vendors, delivery personnel, even clerks at the county building—made her step back, certain they carried some silent threat. Over time, the office became a maze of calculated detours. She avoided the main stairwell where maintenance crews worked with clattering tools, opting instead for the long elevator ride down three additional floors, a delay that accumulated in missed deadlines and quiet tension with her supervisor. At home, she and Robert stopped sitting on the same sofa. She could not bear his hand resting on her shoulder, could not tolerate even a casual brush of his arm against hers. The moment skin touched skin, her breath would catch, and she would pull away as though burned. When a friend suggested a routine check-up, Clara declined, then declined the follow-up calls. Hospitals, ambulances, the sterile scent of antiseptic, the weight of a clinical exam—all of it triggered a quiet, vibrating dread that made her cancel appointments hours before they began. Talking about the event became its own obstacle; each time she attempted to voice it, the narrative fractured before she could finish. She would start describing the corridor, then the air, then the noise, but each attempt dissolved into a fog of disconnected images and physical sensations. She could not put the frightening event into language; it lived entirely in her nerves. Now, at fifty-one, Clara sits in a quiet waiting room, her hands folded tightly in her lap. She has come because the narrow circle of places where she feels safe has become impossible to maintain. Her husband notices how she flinches at the sound of a dropped file, how she leaves office meetings early when voices rise. She is ready to speak, not because the memory has softened, but because the weight of carrying it alone has grown too heavy. What frightened her most was losing the last fragments of stability she had clung to; what she hoped for, quietly, was to find a way to walk through a crowded room without bracing for impact.
